historical_timeline.summary: Born at Żelazowa Wola; the family moved to Warsaw within months.
Recurrent cough, fever, headaches, and swollen glands in his teens.
His youngest sister died of tuberculosis.
Settled in Paris, where he earned his living mainly by teaching.
An engagement made conditional on his health; met George Sand; seriously ill the following winter.
Arrived on Majorca; gravely ill at Valldemossa through the winter.
Chest pain, hemoptysis, and breathlessness later in life.
Last concert, in London, despite frailty and fever.
Two hemorrhages; tuberculosis diagnosed in its final stage.
Cystic fibrosis and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency proposed as retrospective diagnoses.
Macroscopic examination of his preserved heart.
Heart failure with cirrhosis proposed as an alternative cause of death.

claims.statement: Fryderyk Franciszek Chopin was born in the village of Żelazowa Wola, in Mazovia, on March 1, 1810, according to his own statements and his family's; his baptismal certificate, written several weeks after the birth, gives February 22.

His father, Mikołaj (Nicolas) Chopin, was a Frenchman from Lorraine who settled permanently in Poland and brought up his children as Poles; the family moved to Warsaw a few months after Fryderyk's birth.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his Polish and French background.

claims.statement: In 1827 the youngest of the Chopin children, his sister Emilia, died of tuberculosis.
A review of the documentary sources reports recurrent episodes of cough, fever, headaches, and swollen lymph nodes beginning in his teens.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the lifelong chest illness behind the presenting problem.

claims.statement: He left Warsaw on November 2, 1830, never to return, reached Paris in September 1831, and in 1834 chose the status of a political refugee rather than apply to the Russian embassy for a passport.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his life away from his homeland in the modern social history.

claims.statement: In Paris his most important source of income was giving lessons; he became a popular teacher, and although ranked among the greatest pianists of his time, he disliked public performances, appeared rarely, and preferred an intimate group of listeners.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports his modern occupation as a pianist who earns his living by teaching.

claims.statement: In 1836 a proposal of marriage was accepted on condition that he take better care of his health; the engagement ended a year later, the family of his fiancée being disturbed by the bad state of his health, as he had been seriously ill in the winter.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented frailty and a serious winter illness before the index date.

claims.statement: He met the writer George Sand in Paris in 1836; their relationship, which began soon after, lasted nearly ten years.

In the winter of 1838 to 1839 he stayed on Majorca, arriving in Palma on November 8, 1838. In early December the rented villa became cold and damp, his health worsened, and doctors were called; he wrote on December 3 that he had become "sick as a dog" over the previous two weeks. Neighbors fearing an infectious disease led the owner to force them to leave. At the former Carthusian monastery in Valldemossa, from December 15 to February 11, he became gravely ill and showed symptoms of tuberculosis, and for many weeks was too weak to leave the house, yet composed most of the 24 Preludes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented crisis of his chest illness, after the index date.

claims.statement: On Majorca he suffered long periods of doubt and depression, associated with his illness, and the hostility of local people who feared his illness worsened his state of mind.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Low mood with illness and stigma, in the lay words of the source; not a diagnosis.

claims.statement: After Majorca he convalesced in Marseille from late February to May 1839, cared for by a physician, and moved to Nohant in central France still greatly weakened.
The final parting from George Sand in July 1847 and the loss of Nohant had a devastating effect on his mental and physical state, and he almost gave up composing.

From April to November 1848 he toured England and Scotland; the travel, the many performances, and a climate harmful to his lungs further damaged his health, and on November 16, 1848, despite frailty and a fever, he gave his last concert, in London.
In 1849, after two hemorrhages on June 22, a physician diagnosed tuberculosis in its final stage.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis made in his lifetime.

claims.statement: He died on October 17, 1849, in his apartment on the Place Vendôme in Paris, of pulmonary tuberculosis according to the Fryderyk Chopin Institute, and was buried in the Père-Lachaise cemetery; at his request his heart was taken to Warsaw and placed in a pillar of the Holy Cross Church.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; the modern episode ends in cure.

claims.statement: A macroscopic examination of his preserved heart in 2014 found it enlarged and covered with a fibrinous coating with multiple small nodular foci, which the examiners interpreted as tuberculous pericarditis; they concluded that chronic tuberculosis was the most plausible diagnosis and that rapidly progressing tuberculous pericarditis was probably the immediate cause of death. An earlier review of his case history also judged tuberculosis the most probable diagnosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports the choice of pulmonary tuberculosis as the modern diagnosis; the heart was examined without tissue or microbiological testing in the cited abstracts.

claims.statement: Cystic fibrosis has been proposed as the cause of his lifelong illness and death; the roster lists a "probable cystic fibrosis variant." The heart examination's authors later argued that the disease was infectious, not genetic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Unproven alternative; addressed in the modern episode with a sweat chloride test and not adopted.

claims.statement: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency has also been proposed, while noting that the lost autopsy record makes any diagnosis hard to confirm.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Unproven alternative; addressed in the modern episode with a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level and not adopted.

claims.statement: The same review reports that later in life he had chest pain, hemoptysis, hematemesis, neuralgia, and joint pain, and that exhaustion and breathlessness characterized all his adult life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchor for the hemoptysis and frailty of the presenting illness; the dated hemoptysis comes after the index date.

claims.statement: Another documentary review proposed that he had dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure and cirrhosis, rather than tuberculosis, as the cause of death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Alternative interpretation recorded for completeness; not used.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Chronic cough with hemoptysis and weight loss in a 28-year-old pianist and piano teacher: chest X-ray and CT, three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification, culture and drug susceptibility, an interferon-gamma release assay, HIV and hepatitis testing, home airborne isolation and same-day public-health reporting; the presenting problem resolved into a diagnosis of drug-susceptible cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis; an honest test of the proposed alternatives for his lifelong chest illness (sweat chloride for cystic fibrosis and a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level), both normal; treatment with the four-month rifapentine, moxifloxacin, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide regimen by video-observed therapy under the 1834 CDC interim guidance and the ATS/CDC/IDSA guidelines, with eligibility, weight-band dosing, baseline and monitoring tests, and the 119-dose completion rule; release from isolation and return to teaching; a contact investigation led by the health department; care for moderate malnutrition; attention to low mood and the stigma he fears; and an honest record of a missed monthly symptom check.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Chopin returns three days after his first visit, masked and seen in an airborne infection isolation room, for his results; Dr. Kowalczyk-Grant of infectious diseases sees him the same morning. He has stayed at home with no students or visitors, and his lessons have moved online. His cough and night sweats are unchanged, and he has coughed up streaks of blood once since the first visit. His three sputum smears show acid-fast bacilli (2+, 2+, and 1+), and the nucleic acid amplification test on the first sample detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex with no rifampin resistance; molecular tests for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance and the cultures are pending. The interferon-gamma release assay is positive, HIV is negative, hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody are negative with surface antibody positive from vaccination, and hepatitis C antibody is negative. He was relieved to have a name for the illness and asked how long treatment lasts and when he can teach again. After the four-month and six-month regimens were explained, he chose the four-month regimen and took his first observed dose with a meal in the clinic.

assessment_plan.assessment: Confirmed today, replacing the presenting problem of cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. No rifampin resistance. He meets the criteria for the four-month regimen: over 12 years old, weight 48.4 kg (at least 40 kg), pulmonary disease only, HIV negative, no prolonged QT history and no QT-prolonging or interacting medicines, normal potassium (4.0), magnesium (2.0), liver tests, and creatinine, no earlier tuberculosis treatment, and specimens sent for susceptibility testing before the first dose. Dr. Kowalczyk-Grant agrees
plan: Rifapentine 1200 mg, moxifloxacin 400 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, and pyrazinamide 1000 mg daily with food for eight weeks, then rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and isoniazid for nine weeks, with pyridoxine 50 mg, by video-observed therapy seven days a week
Three sputum smears in the third week for the release decision; then monthly sputum until two cultures are negative
Liver tests in two to three weeks because of his low weight and albumin; stop the doses and call the same day for yellow eyes, dark urine, vomiting, or abdominal pain
Stop moxifloxacin and call for tendon pain; report numbness or tingling in his fingers
No mineral supplements, antacids, or zinc products within four hours before or eight hours after the dose

referral.question: Suspected cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis in a 28-year-old pianist and piano teacher with three months of cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, and weight loss, and a lifelong history of chest illness. Please confirm the diagnosis when the sputum results return, advise on the regimen, monitoring, and his return to teaching, and tell us whether cystic fibrosis or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency needs to be excluded
referral.urgency: Urgent, on the day the sputum results return (expected within three days)
referral.pertinent_history: Cough for three months, blood streaks for two weeks, evening fevers, night sweats, and weight loss of about 6 kg to 48.5 kg (BMI 16.8). Temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 102, oxygen saturation 95 percent. Recurrent coughs and fevers since his teens. Born in Poland; lives alone and teaches about fifteen students a week, teenagers and adults, in his apartment. Chest X-ray and CT: a 2.5 cm thick-walled right upper lobe cavity with tree-in-bud nodules in both upper lobes; no bronchiectasis, emphysema, or enlarged nodes. Three sputum samples sent for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification, culture, and susceptibility; interferon-gamma release assay, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C tests sent. Hemoglobin 12.1 (low), platelets 442 (high), albumin 3.2 (low), ALT 18, AST 24, bilirubin 0.5, creatinine 0.78, potassium 4.0, calcium 9.0, magnesium 2.0. PHQ-9 7, item 9 scored 0; AUDIT-C 2. No medicines; no known allergies. Home airborne isolation started, lessons moved online, and the suspected case reported to the health department today
questions: Do the results confirm pulmonary tuberculosis, and does anything else need to be considered?
Is he eligible for the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen, and would you choose it over the six-month regimen?
What monitoring does he need, given his low weight and albumin?
When can he leave isolation and teach his students again?
Should cystic fibrosis or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency be tested for, given his lifelong chest illness?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Chopin, a 28-year-old pianist who teaches in his apartment, is seen at the request of Dr. Lindqvist three days after presenting with three months of cough, two weeks of blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, evening fevers, and weight loss. He has coughed up blood once more since. He has had recurrent coughs and fevers with colds since his teens, but he has never had a diagnosis of a chronic lung disease, nasal polyps, sinus disease, greasy stools, or liver disease. He has never been treated for tuberculosis and knows of no contact with drug-resistant disease. He takes no medicines and has no history of heart rhythm problems or fainting
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Lindqvist's note; the chest X-ray and CT; three sputum smears (2+, 2+, 1+); the nucleic acid amplification test (Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex detected, rifampin resistance not detected); the interferon-gamma release assay (positive); HIV-1/2 antigen and antibody (negative); hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody (negative) with surface antibody positive; hepatitis C antibody (negative); and the baseline blood count, liver and kidney tests, potassium, calcium, and magnesium

exam.finding: Thin and tired; temperature 37.6 °C, pulse 98; seen in an airborne infection isolation room
Coarse crackles and bronchial breathing over the right upper zone; fine crackles at the left apex
Normal sensation in the fingers and feet

assessment.assessment: Confirmed by a positive amplification test with three positive smears, in keeping with the cavity and the symptoms. No rifampin resistance. A positive interferon-gamma release assay supports the diagnosis but would not have excluded it if negative. Nontuberculous mycobacteria do not give a positive amplification test for the tuberculosis complex. Cultures, molecular tests for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance, and phenotypic susceptibility are pending

He is eligible for the four-month regimen: age over 12, weight 48.4 kg, pulmonary disease only, HIV negative, no prolonged QT history or QT-prolonging medicines, normal potassium and magnesium, normal liver tests and creatinine, no earlier treatment, and specimens sent for susceptibility before the first dose. A cavity does not exclude it. Compared with the six-month regimen it shortens treatment by two months, which matters to him as a teacher and performer, at the cost of more tablets taken with food and the moxifloxacin precautions. He chose it after hearing both options

An electrocardiogram is not routinely needed, because he has no QT risk factors. His low weight and albumin justify one early liver check even without symptoms. Moxifloxacin can cause tendon injury and, with isoniazid, nerve damage, which would matter greatly to a pianist; both should be asked about at every visit and every observed dose

assessment.display: Cystic fibrosis and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
assessment.assessment: Neither is likely: the CT shows no bronchiectasis or emphysema, he has no sinus or pancreatic symptoms, and tuberculosis fully explains his illness. Because his lifelong chest illness raises the question and he wants it answered, a sweat chloride test and a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level are reasonable and simple; a sweat chloride below 30 mmol/L makes cystic fibrosis unlikely
Undernutrition raises the risk of poor outcomes and drug toxicity; pyridoxine is needed with isoniazid

recommendations: Start today: rifapentine 1200 mg, moxifloxacin 400 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, and pyrazinamide 1000 mg (weight band 40 to under 55 kg) once daily with food for eight weeks (56 doses), then rifapentine, moxifloxacin, and isoniazid for nine weeks (63 doses), with pyridoxine 50 mg, all by video-observed therapy seven days a week; the regimen is complete at 119 doses, with the intensive phase within 70 days and the whole regimen within five months

No mineral supplements, antacids, or zinc products within four hours before or eight hours after the dose; review any new medicine for interactions with rifapentine or for QT effects with moxifloxacin
Liver tests in two to three weeks and at once for hepatitis symptoms; stop the doses and call for ALT above three times the upper limit with symptoms or five times without
Ask about tendon pain and numbness or tingling at every visit; stop moxifloxacin for tendon pain

Three sputum smears in the third week for release from isolation; monthly sputum culture until two are negative, including the two-month culture; send any positive two-month culture for repeat susceptibility testing
Phenotypic susceptibility to rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and moxifloxacin on the first isolate; change the regimen if any resistance is found
Sweat chloride test and serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level at the next visit, once he is out of isolation
Dietitian support with supplement drinks taken in the afternoon or evening, away from the dose
No electrocardiogram unless symptoms or a new QT-prolonging medicine arise
I will review the results by message at two months and at the end of treatment; no further infectious diseases visit unless the cultures stay positive, resistance is found, or a drug must be stopped
